newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Wolters Kluwer H1 net profit up 21 pct.
newsitem.headline: Wolters Kluwer H1 net profit up 21 pct.

text.p: Dutch business publisher Wolters Kluwer NV reported a 21 percent increase in net profit for the first half of 1997 on Tuesday, right in line with expectations.
The company said net profit rose to 244 million guilders from 202 million. A Reuters poll of analysts before the results had produced a consensus forecast of 245 million guilders.
Operational cash flow, viewed by many analysts as a better performance gauge, rose 55 percent to 554 million guilders.
Wolters Kluwer operates in 25 countries with core activities in legal, tax, business, medical and science publishing.
"Measured in local currencies, nearly all countries contributed to the growth in sales and results," the company said in a statement.
First-half sales came to 2.42 billion guilders, up 20 percent on the same period of 1996.
Acquisitions and currency effects, particularly the stronger dollar, helped to fuel the growth of sales and profits.
A company spokeswoman said acquisitions had raised sales by some 10 percent, while currency translation effects had boosted sales by some five percent.
However, not all of the rise in the dollar versus the guilder translates directly into higher profits as the company has substantial amounts of dollar-denominated debt.
Financing charges rose 24 percent in the first half of this year to 102 million guilders, due to the dollar's appreciation and ongoing acquisitions.
Wolters Kluwer said it was particularly pleased with the performance of its U.S. subsidiaries, adding that restructuring of U.S. tax publisher CCH, acquired in 1996, was going to plan.

In Europe, adjustments of the group's Swedish educational publishing business were starting to bear fruit while results in France were boosted by the integration of legal, transport and pharmacology publisher Groupe Liaisons, acquired in late 1996.
Subsidiaries in the Asia-Pacific region, including recently acquired New Zealand based medical publisher Adis, had fully met management's expectations, the company said.
Wolters Kluwer said it would continue to develop electronic media, but added that in many cases such products would complement traditional print products rather than replace them.
